entry.title: Vector: The Rust Router That Moves Your LLM’s Logs, Metrics, and Traces

link.title: Vector: The Rust Router That Moves Your LLM’s Logs, Metrics, and Traces

entry.content:
Ask anyone running a large language model service what their telemetry situation looks like and watch them wince. A single serving cluster can emit millions of structured log lines per day — prompts, completions, tool calls, guardrail verdicts — plus metrics like tokens per second, time to first token, and GPU utilization, plus traces for every step an agent takes. Where all of that lands, and at what fidelity, decides whether you can debug a regression at 3 a.m. or only guess at it. Vector, maintained by Datadog under the vectordotdev organization, is the Rust-powered engine that has become one of the most credible answers to that routing problem.

The README’s opening describes Vector as a high-performance, end-to-end agent and aggregator for observability data that lets you collect, transform, and route your logs and metrics to any vendor you want today — and any other vendor tomorrow. Three claims matter for AI infrastructure work. First, reliability: the project states that its primary design goal is reliability, and it is built in memory-safe Rust. Second, reach: the README reports over 100,000 downloads per day and a largest user processing more than 500 terabytes daily. Third, neutrality: the same event stream can fan out to storage, streaming, and monitoring systems at once, which is exactly the posture an ML platform team wants when it must feed a metrics store, a log lake, and an evaluation warehouse simultaneously.

This post is a source tour, not a paraphrase of marketing pages. Every symbol and line number below was read directly from the master branch of the repository at the time of writing. We will walk two generated architecture diagrams — an overview of the data path and a deeper map of the internals — then trace the handshake that carries a config file from disk to a running topology, stand up a first flow using the starter config that ships inside the repo, and finish with an honest list of limits.

Vector at a glance: configuration flows down through validation into the topology builder, while events flow from sources through transforms to sinks.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Loading starts at load_from_paths_with_provider_and_secrets, L185, which discovers candidate files, interpolates environment variables, and expands secret backends before anything else runs.
  • The parsed result becomes the Config struct, L155 — the whole topology expressed as data: sources, transforms, sinks, and global options.
  • Before anything starts, check_shape, L93 and its siblings for names, resources, outputs, and buffer preconditions reject impossible topologies with a list of plain errors rather than one cryptic failure.
  • TopologyPiecesBuilder::build, L1174 then assembles the validated config into buffers, fan-out handles, and component tasks.
  • The assembled pieces are handed to RunningTopology::start_init_validated, L1421, which spawns the live machinery and watches for graceful crashes.
  • On schema-aware setups, possible_definitions, L30 merges output schemas across the graph, so mis-typed wiring fails at startup instead of at 2 a.m.
  • In the transform slot, RemapConfig, L58 compiles VRL programs — the small language where most real-world parsing lives.
  • For live inspection, GrpcServer::start, L58 serves the topology API behind vector top, while tap, L42 streams a sample of flowing events straight to your terminal.

The deeper map: the loading chain and validation on the left, the topology runtime in the middle, the API, tap, and internal metrics as the control plane, and the component zoo on the right.

Why a Telemetry Fabric Belongs in Your AI Stack

An LLM application emits three event shapes at once, and most homegrown setups handle them with three half-maintained scripts. Vector’s answer is a single event model flowing through typed ports: a source produces events, transforms reshape them, and sinks deliver them, all wired in one declarative file. The OpenTelemetry source speaks OTLP over gRPC and HTTP, so instrumenting with the usual SDKs works out of the box. If you already run the OpenTelemetry Collector you can think of Vector as a sibling with a different center of gravity — both ingest OTLP (see our /opentelemetry-collector/ tour), but Vector adds the VRL transform language and ships as one static Rust binary.

The fan-out is where AI platforms benefit most. The same stream can feed a Prometheus-compatible store for serving metrics (/prometheus/), a log lake for prompt auditing (/loki/), and Kafka for downstream eval or training jobs (/kafka/) without triple-reading from the source. VRL then does the boring, critical work: scrub PII from prompt bodies, tag events with model name and customer tier, convert log-shaped metrics into real metrics, and drop noise before it becomes someone’s storage bill.

Reliability under load is the quiet differentiator. Sinks batch events through a payload Buffer, L22 that compresses with gzip, zlib, zstd, or snappy before delivery, and validation checks buffer preconditions before startup so a mis-sized disk buffer fails loudly instead of silently swallowing events. Batch and training jobs benefit from the same mechanics: the file source tails long-running job logs, the reduce transform merges per-job event streams into running summaries, and the route transform splits evaluation traffic from production traffic so one noisy experiment cannot flood a shared store. Because the binary is static Rust, the same artifact plays both roles the README describes — an agent on every GPU node and a central aggregator — without a second toolchain.

The Config-to-Running Handshake

Reloads are where routing engines usually fall over, so it is worth seeing how Vector does it. Every start and every reload passes through a diff: ConfigDiff, L9 records which components changed, were added, or were removed between the old and new configs. The shared TopologyController, L43 exposes a reload entry point that runs the new config through validation and only then calls reload_config_and_respawn, L312 to replace exactly the components that need replacing. With the --watch-config flag, verified at watch_config, L180, the config watcher triggers that cycle automatically on file changes.

Each component future is wrapped in a Task, L81 that converts panics and errors into typed outcomes, so one crashing sink does not silently poison the process — the running topology observes the failure and can shut the process down deliberately rather than limping along. The same machinery powers config unit tests: UnitTest::run, L73 builds throwaway topologies from test cases and asserts on their outputs without shipping any traffic, which is why routing logic in Vector configs can be reviewed like ordinary code. Stop the world with TopologyController::stop, L162 and Vector drains gracefully, bounded by the --graceful-shutdown-limit-secs default of 60 seconds documented in the CLI.

From Install to Your First Model

Vector installs from the quickstart linked at the top of the README, or from the distribution/install.sh script that ships in the repo root; container definitions live under distribution/docker (alpine, debian, and distroless variants), and the repo also carries Kubernetes manifests for a DaemonSet agent and a StatefulSet aggregator under distribution/kubernetes.

The fastest first flow needs no external service at all, because the repo ships a starter config at config/vector.yaml that generates syslog-formatted demo logs, parses them with a VRL remap transform — parse_syslog!(string!(.message)) — and prints pretty JSON to the console:

sources:
  dummy_logs:
    type: "demo_logs"
    format: "syslog"
    interval: 1
transforms:
  parse_logs:
    type: "remap"
    inputs: ["dummy_logs"]
    source: |
      . = parse_syslog!(string!(.message))
sinks:
  print:
    type: "console"
    inputs: ["parse_logs"]
    encoding:
      codec: "json"
      json:
        pretty: true

Point the binary at it with the --config-yaml flag (the CLI also accepts TOML and JSON, and wildcards are supported), and you have a running flow in seconds. Two more subcommands make exploration easy: vector list enumerates every source, transform, and sink your build supports, and vector generate scaffolds a config stub for a chosen component so you never start from an empty file. Before starting anything real, run vector validate — the subcommand exists in the CLI alongside generate, list, test, top, tap, and vrl — and treat vector test as your CI gate: it executes assertions defined directly inside your config through the unit test harness, so routing logic gets regression-checked like any other code. When you are ready to watch it breathe, enable the API block and use vector top; for a live sample of events, vector tap is one command away. If a sink must be reachable before traffic flows, start with --require-healthy and Vector will exit rather than pretend everything is fine.

Honest Limits

The performance story deserves a careful eye. The “up to 10x faster than every alternative” line in the README is backed by a public test harness, but the harness’s own table shows nuance: Vector wins TCP to Blackhole at 86 MiB/s, yet in Regex Parsing FluentBit leads at 20.5 MiB/s against Vector’s 13.2. Directionally fast, workload-dependent — benchmark your own path.

Scope caveats matter too. The README’s feature table marks metrics with a beta label and traces with a construction sign described as coming soon, even though the OTLP source already decodes span batches; the unified three-signal story is still maturing at the edges. Healthchecks are per-sink rather than universal — Loki, CloudWatch Logs, and New Relic ship probes — so --require-healthy only protects you for sinks that have one. The embedded API is disabled by default, which surprises people who run vector top first and see nothing. Finally, the headline adoption numbers — downloads per day, the 500-terabyte user — are project-reported, not independently audited. None of this is disqualifying; it just means you should verify against your workloads the way you would for any infrastructure component.

What makes Vector durable is architectural honesty: config as data, validation before startup, diffs before reloads, and a transform language that is itself testable. For teams standing up LLM services, that combination turns telemetry routing from a pile of scripts into reviewed, versioned, regression-tested code — which is precisely the standard we hold the models themselves to.
entry.summary: A verified source tour of vectordotdev/vector — the Rust engine that collects, transforms, and routes observability data — with two architecture diagrams and line-anchored code links.

entry.title: Zipkin Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Tracing System That Started It All

link.title: Zipkin Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Tracing System That Started It All

entry.content:
Every AI stack you operate today — an API gateway routing to a model server, an agent orchestrating tool calls, a RAG chain fanning out to an embedding service and a vector database — creates the same debugging problem Zipkin was invented to solve. A single user request touches a dozen services, and when the whole thing takes eight seconds instead of eight hundred milliseconds, you need to know exactly which hop burned the time. Zipkin, originally built at Twitter and now shepherded by the OpenZipkin community, is the project that defined the trace-and-span vocabulary almost every observability tool still speaks, including the telemetry sidecars you deploy next to inference clusters.

The vocabulary is worth restating because it is everywhere now: a trace is a tree of spans; a span is a named, timed operation carrying a trace ID, a span ID, a parent span ID, timestamps, and tags. When a framework promises to “trace your inference call chain,” it is emitting Zipkin-shaped data, whether it says so or not. The data model in zipkin2.Span — trace ID, parent ID, kind, endpoints, duration, tags — is the original contract client libraries worldwide compile against.

Why read the source? Because for AI and ML infrastructure, tracing is not a nice-to-have: token-by-token generation makes latency distributions heavy-tailed, and a waterfall of spans is often the only honest way to see whether the retrieval step, the reranker, or the model itself ate the budget. Zipkin is also a masterclass in restrained Java design: a small collector core, hand-rolled wire codecs, a single storage SPI, and a query API thin enough to read in one sitting. Understanding it makes its successors legible too — Jaeger re-imagined the tracer for the CNCF era, and the modern OpenTelemetry Collector inherits the same receive-decode-store shape. In this post we walk the actual Java source of openzipkin/zipkin on master (commit 878ce2a1, November 2026) and follow bytes from the front door to storage and back out.

Zipkin at a glance: two transport entry points (HTTP and Kafka) feed one transport-neutral collector, which decodes, samples, and stores spans through a storage SPI; the query API v2 reads them back as JSON.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • ZipkinServer, L33 — the entire server is a Spring Boot application; main() merely builds a SpringApplicationBuilder with a custom banner and module importers, then runs.
  • EnableZipkinServer, L18 — one annotation, @Import(InternalZipkinConfiguration), activates every internal bean: collectors, storage adapters, health checks, and the query API.
  • uploadSpans, L59 — @Post("/api/v2/spans"), with sibling methods for protobuf and for v1 JSON/thrift clients, all routed to the same validation method.
  • validateAndStoreSpans, L96 — aggregates the request body, checks that it decodes as the expected format, then moves the work off the event loop onto a blocking executor.
  • KafkaCollectorWorker.run, L57 — the Kafka path: a one-second polling loop that feeds every record into the very same Collector, being deliberately lenient with malformed bytes.
  • Collector.acceptSpans, L134 — the transport-neutral funnel: decode bytes into Span objects, sample, and enqueue for storage.
  • SpanBytesDecoderDetector.detectDecoder, L84 — magic-byte sniffing chooses between JSON v1, JSON v2, proto3, and thrift with no content-type header required.
  • getTraces, L114 — the read side: HTTP parameters become a QueryRequest, and the result of storage.spanStore().getTraces(...) is re-encoded as JSON v2.

The detail view: boot wiring, the HTTP and Kafka transports, the collector core, the codec layer, the storage SPI, and the query API, with the exact classes and methods that connect them.

The Collector: One Front Door, Many Transports

Zipkin accepts spans over HTTP, gRPC, and message queues, and the HTTP path is the easiest to read. ZipkinHttpCollector is an Armeria annotated service whose uploadSpans method handles POST /api/v2/spans with JSON v2, while uploadSpansProtobuf and uploadSpansV1Thrift accept other encodings on the same paths, distinguished by content type. Before any decoding, UnzippingBytesRequestConverter.convertRequest (same file, L228) transparently gunzips bodies that arrive with Content-Encoding: gzip and counts the incoming bytes into collector metrics.

The interesting part is how defensive the endpoint is. validateAndStoreSpans runs the payload through SpanBytesDecoderDetector.decoderForListMessage before trusting its declared decoder, and a helper called testForUnexpectedFormat (L169) looks for byte patterns that betray a v1 payload masquerading as v2 — binary annotations and endpoint fields that should not exist. Errors surface synchronously so client developers see mistakes immediately, while storage happens later: the collector hands work to a blockingTaskExecutor and answers through CompletableCallback (L212), completing the response with HTTP 202 once bytes are accepted, not once they are stored.

The Kafka path trades interactivity for throughput. KafkaCollector is a CollectorComponent configured with a topic (default zipkin), bootstrap servers, and a stream count, and it spawns one KafkaCollectorWorker per stream. The worker’s run() loop polls for up to a second, then iterates records: empty messages are skipped, and legacy single-span thrift payloads are detected by first byte and decoded with SpanBytesDecoder.THRIFT.decodeOne before everything else goes through collector.acceptSpans(bytes, NOOP) (L100), which auto-detects the format. Failure is contained per record — a bad message is counted and dropped rather than killing the loop. If you already run Kafka for telemetry fan-in, this transport is a natural fit, and our Kafka deep dive covers the broker side.

Span Processing: Decode, Sample, Store

All transports converge on one small class. Collector in zipkin-collector/core describes itself as the component that “takes action on spans received from a transport,” and its accept method (L107) is the whole policy in twenty lines: count the spans, sample them, swap in a callback that disconnects the caller from storage, and execute a StoreSpans runnable on an executor. The sampling step iterates the batch and asks CollectorSampler.isSampled(traceId, debug) for each trace — decisions are made per trace ID, so all spans of one trace survive or drop together.

StoreSpans (L210) then calls storage.spanConsumer().accept(sampledSpans), which is the only write contract in the system: SpanConsumer.accept (L12) takes a list of spans and returns a Call<Void>. That Call abstraction — a cloneable deferred command with synchronous execute() and asynchronous enqueue(Callback) — keeps storage backends pluggable without async frameworks in the core.

The default backend is the one you get for free: with zipkin.storage.type defaulting to mem (see zipkin-server-shared.yml, L118), InMemoryStorage (L59) implements both SpanStore and SpanConsumer with bounded, query-friendly in-memory collections. Third-party and first-party adapters — Elasticsearch, Cassandra 3, MySQL — plug into the same two interfaces declared by StorageComponent (L22), which is why the server binary can talk to radically different stores without the collector caring.

The Codec Layer: Hand-Rolled Wire Formats

Zipkin does not use a serialization framework for its v2 wire formats; it hand-rolls them for allocation control. SpanBytesEncoder (L17) is a four-value enum — JSON_V1, THRIFT, JSON_V2, PROTO3 — and the JSON v2 value delegates to V2SpanWriter (L18), a field-by-field writer over a reusable WriteBuffer. The protobuf path lives in Proto3Codec (L15), the shared JSON plumbing is JsonCodec (L34). The mirror-image SpanBytesDecoder enum (L24) provides decodeList and decodeOne for each format.

Format detection is the cleverest corner. Because Kafka historically has no content type, mixed-format topics are a real-world problem, and SpanBytesDecoderDetector solves it with heuristics documented right in the source: a first byte at or below 16 means binary (thrift, or proto3 when it matches the varint pattern), a leading [ means a JSON list, and the presence of "localEndpoint"/"remoteEndpoint" or a "tags" field distinguishes v2 JSON from v1. The class comment admits the trick can be fooled — a v1 binary annotation literally named to end in Endpoint — but calls that scenario unlikely in practice thanks to the lc convention.

From Install to Your First Model

The fastest path from zero to a trace is two commands from the project README:

curl -sSL https://zipkin.io/quickstart.sh | bash -s
java -jar zipkin.jar

That fetches the latest zipkin-server executable jar and starts it with in-memory storage. Docker works identically: docker run -d -p 9411:9411 openzipkin/zipkin. The server listens on port 9411 (QUERY_PORT:9411 in zipkin-server-shared.yml), with the UI at the root path.

Now send one hand-written span to the endpoint uploadSpans serves — this mimics what an instrumented service would report for a model-generation step:

curl -s -X POST http://localhost:9411/api/v2/spans \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '[{"traceId":"aaa111aaa111aaa1","id":"bbb222bbb222bbb2",
        "name":"llm generate","localEndpoint":{"serviceName":"inference-api"},
        "timestamp":1793840000000000,"duration":420000,
        "tags":{"model":"qwen2.5-7b","prompt_tokens":"128"}}]'

A successful POST returns HTTP 202 — the status lives in CompletableCallback. Pull the span back out through the query API served by getTrace (L144):

curl -s http://localhost:9411/api/v2/trace/aaa111aaa111aaa1

For a realistic chain, point your instrumented services at Zipkin using Brave or an OpenTelemetry SDK with a Zipkin exporter, or route everything through a collector as described in our OpenTelemetry Collector post. In an LLM stack, name spans after the stages you actually argue about — retrieve, rerank, generate — and tag them with model ID and token counts; the waterfall view then answers the only question that matters at 3 a.m.: which stage burned the latency.

Query API: Reading Traces Back Out

The read side is ZipkinQueryApiV2 (L48), another Armeria annotated service. Its getTraces endpoint maps query parameters onto a QueryRequest — service name, span name, annotation query, min/max duration, end timestamp, lookback, limit — built with the builder at L126, then executes storage.spanStore().getTraces(queryRequest) and encodes the result with SpanBytesEncoder.JSON_V2. Single-trace fetch, trace-many by ID list, service and span name listings (backed by the ServiceAndSpanNames SPI), autocomplete keys, and dependency links (getDependencies, L77) round out the surface. Every storage call returns a Call, so a backend can serve it synchronously from memory or asynchronously over the network without the API layer knowing or caring.

Honest Limits

Everything below is verified against the source or README; no benchmarks here are invented.

  • In-memory storage is the default and is not durable. With STORAGE_TYPE unset you get InMemoryStorage; restart wipes every trace. Production deployments must configure Elasticsearch, Cassandra 3, or MySQL.
  • The slim distribution drops message transports. The README states it supports in-memory and Elasticsearch storage only — the full jar is required for Kafka or RabbitMQ.
  • Sampling is lossy by design. Collector.sample (L197) silently drops spans whose trace IDs fail isSampled, and head-sampling decisions made upstream mean incompletely reported chains if your services disagree on rates.
  • The query window defaults to one day. defaultLookback is 86400000 ms (L64), so older traces exist in storage but are not returned unless the client widens lookback.
  • Format detection is heuristic. The detector’s own comments document cases where hand-crafted payloads can masquerade as another encoding; it is a convenience for messy transports, not a security boundary.
  • Zipkin traces; it does not do metrics or logs. It is one leg of the observability tripod — pair it with a metrics store like Prometheus and a log system, and for object-store-first trace storage at scale, see our Tempo write-up.

Zipkin rewards source reading because it is small: two transports, one collector, four encodings, two storage interfaces, one query API. The next time your inference gateway traces a request through retriever and model server, you know the exact Java those spans wade through — and the vocabulary was drafted in this repository.
entry.summary: A guided tour through the openzipkin/zipkin Java source: how the HTTP and Kafka collectors decode spans, how sampling works, and how the query API reads traces back out.

entry.title: Arroyo Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Rust SQL Streaming Engine

link.title: Arroyo Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Rust SQL Streaming Engine

entry.content:
Modern machine learning is increasingly a streaming problem. Models that score fraud, rank feeds, or trigger alerts do not want a nightly table dump — they want fresh features computed continuously over the same event streams that drive the product. Arroyo is a distributed stream processing engine written in Rust that attacks exactly this layer: you write SQL, and it performs stateful computations over bounded and unbounded sources, emitting results as soon as they arrive. Its README lists “Real-time ML feature generation” as a first-class use case, alongside fraud detection and real-time ingestion into data lakes.

Why does a streaming engine belong in an AI infrastructure stack? Because feature computation is the connective tissue between raw events and model serving. Rolling counts, per-session aggregations, and sliding averages over a Kafka topic are precisely the shapes a windowed SQL query expresses well — and they must run continuously, survive failures, and never silently lose an epoch of data. A Kafka-API broker such as Redpanda supplies the durable log; Arroyo turns that log into features. Batch-oriented companions like Materialize and RisingWave solve adjacent parts of the real-time SQL space, but Arroyo’s design is deliberately dataflow-first: SQL is compiled into a distributed graph, not a continuously-refreshed view.

This post walks the master branch of the repository the way the code executes: the SQL-to-DAG compiler in arroyo-planner, the serializable graph model in arroyo-datastream, the Arrow-based runtime in arroyo-worker and arroyo-operator, checkpointing in arroyo-state and arroyo-storage, and the extension layers — connectors and UDFs. Every symbol cited below was verified against the source tree, and the two diagrams were generated from the actual file structure.

Overview: SQL text flows through the DataFusion-backed planner into a logical graph, the chaining optimizer fuses stages, and the Arrow runtime executes subtasks with checkpointed state, connectors on both edges.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything is one Rust binary. The Commands, L82 enum offers run, api, controller, cluster, worker, node, and a plan Visualize subcommand.
  • The compiler entry point is parse_and_get_program, L614 — it parses SQL and plans it through DataFusion.
  • PlanToGraphVisitor, L47 walks the resulting plan and collects operators into a graph.
  • LogicalProgram, L300 is the serializable DAG; ChainingOptimizer, L18 fuses compatible neighbors to cut network hops.
  • On workers, Engine, L373 builds the physical graph and start (L528) spawns every subtask.
  • Each stage implements ArrowOperator, L1153, processing Arrow RecordBatch streams.
  • WorkerJobController, L46 drives job lifecycle and checkpoint timing.
  • TableManager, L37 snapshots keyed state per epoch into parquet files written through the StorageProvider (L56) on S3, R2, GCS, Azure, or local disk.
  • On the edges, KafkaConnector, L71 moves bytes, while UdfDylib, L168 loads user functions into running tasks.

Detail: the operator library, checkpoint mechanics, connector construction, and UDF loading, each anchored to verified files and line numbers.

In the detail view, the upper band is the compilation funnel, the middle band is the operator library that DataFusion-generated stages resolve into, and the lower bands carry durability and IO. Edges are labeled with the mechanism each hop uses — control messages, barrier propagation, batch delivery — and every box points at the exact file and line in the repository, so the diagram doubles as a reading list.

SQL In, Dataflow Out: the Compiler Path

Arroyo accepts SQL as text, either from the CLI or the API server. parse_sql, L880 tokenizes it with sqlparser through a custom ArroyoDialect. The statements are then executed against an ArroyoSchemaProvider, L118 that exposes tables backed by connectors plus the built-in function registry assembled by register_functions (L135).

User-defined functions join the session in two flavors: add_rust_udf (L329) accepts Rust source, and add_python_udf (L412) accepts Python — both are parsed at compile time so the engine knows each function’s signature before a single event flows.

DataFusion plans the query, and that is where the streaming translation happens. PlanToGraphVisitor visits each plan node — including Arroyo’s own extensions for sinks, windows, key calculation, and updating aggregates — and emits LogicalNode, L220 vertices wired by LogicalEdge, L136 edges into a petgraph DAG. The final LogicalProgram is binary-serializable, which is what lets a controller ship the compiled job to remote workers unchanged. Before handoff, ChainingOptimizer rewrites the graph (its Optimizer impl at L40) to fuse chainable stages, so a filter followed by a projection runs in one task with zero serialization between them. For library embedding rather than SQL text, parse_and_get_arrow_program (L884) exposes the same machinery programmatically.

The Runtime: Arrow Batches, Not Rows

Workers never see SQL. Engine, L373 receives the logical graph, and Program::from_logical (L210) expands every node into one subtask per parallelism slot — restoring checkpoint metadata first if the job is recovering from a stored epoch. construct_operator (L903) then instantiates each stage from a registry of constructors.

Two traits define the programming model. SourceOperator, L329 owns the head of the graph: it collects records, broadcasts watermarks, and stamps barriers. ArrowOperator, L1153 is the workhorse: on_start, process_batch, handle_watermark, and handle_checkpoint callbacks over columnar batches. Subtasks exchange batches over the network via Quad addressing (network_manager.rs, L272).

The window implementations show how much care went into Arrow-native design: TumblingAggregatingWindowFunc, L50 and SlidingAggregatingWindowFunc, L46 aggregate in fixed and overlapping panes, IncrementalAggregatingFunc, L201 maintains updating results without recomputing, and LookupJoin, L37 enriches streams from dimension tables. Event-time correctness comes from WatermarkGenerator, L35, which advances watermarks batch by batch. Pure row expressions are pushed straight into DataFusion physical plans via StatelessPhysicalExecutor (L287 in arrow/mod.rs).

Checkpoints: Parquet State and Two-Phase Commits

Fault tolerance is the most instructive part of the codebase. The WorkerJobController periodically calls its checkpoint method (L774), which starts a new epoch. A CheckpointBarrier, L492 — the epoch marker — then sweeps through the graph.

When a barrier reaches a subtask, run_checkpoint (operator.rs, L308) asks TableManager to snapshot all keyed tables via its checkpoint method (L368) and reports a FinishedSync event upstream. CheckpointState, L26 accumulates those acks (checkpoint_event, L217), assembles CheckpointMetadata (build_metadata, L416), and — once every subtask has reported — flips into CommittingState, L6 through into_commit (L475). The controller’s send_commit_messages (L794) then commits: a two-phase protocol so sinks publish only after the whole graph agrees the epoch is durable.

The state itself is ordinary parquet. StateBackend is a type alias for ParquetBackend, L25 (see the alias at state/lib.rs, L54), and files land on StorageProvider — S3, R2, GCS, Azure, or local paths (config structs at L199-L228). Because checkpoint files are just parquet, they are inspectable and debuggable with ordinary tooling, a small but real operational win.

Connectors and UDFs: the Extension Points

The IO layer separates configuration from execution. Connection, L23 models a profile plus table config, and every connector implements the Connector, L68 trait; a connectors registry (L39 in arroyo-connectors/src/lib.rs) exposes them by name. The repository ships Kafka, Kinesis, NATS, MQTT, Fluvio, Redis, WebSocket, Webhook, HTTP polling, impulse, and filesystem connectors — the latter writing parquet, JSON, Delta, or Iceberg tables.

Kafka is the canonical example. KafkaConnector, L71 implements Connector (L170) with a from_config factory (L199). Its source half, KafkaSourceFunc, L32, implements SourceOperator (L298); get_consumer (L55) builds the rdkafka consumer, and consumer offsets are persisted as KafkaState (L49) with each checkpoint epoch, so recovery resumes exactly where the last commit left off.

UDFs follow a compile-and-load pattern. The #[udf] proc macro (udf-macros, L62) generates wrappers and type metadata; ParsedUdfFile, L53 parses the submitted Rust source; UdfDylib, L168 loads the compiled library into the task, with an async variant AsyncUdfDylib (L257) for IO-bound functions. Python functions run through PythonUDF, L29 in an embedded interpreter with pyarrow exchange.

From Install to Your First Model

Arroyo ships as a single binary. On macOS use brew install arroyosystems/tap/arroyo, on macOS or Linux run curl -LsSf https://arroyo.dev/install.sh | sh, or start it in Docker with docker run -p 5115:5115 ghcr.io/arroyosystems/arroyo:latest. Launch arroyo cluster and open the web UI at http://localhost:5115; for one local job without the cluster, arroyo run takes a query file directly (RunArgs at L59, executed by run, L400).

Your first “model” does not need a GPU — it needs features. The repository’s own analytics_tutorial.sql test fixture shows the query shape over a Kafka topic; adapted, it computes one-minute rolling hit counts per URL, exactly the kind of input a ranking model consumes:

CREATE TABLE events (
    time TIMESTAMP,
    path TEXT
) WITH (
    connector = 'kafka',
    format = 'json',
    type = 'source',
    bootstrap_servers = 'localhost:9092',
    topic = 'events'
);

CREATE TABLE features (
    time TIMESTAMP,
    path TEXT,
    hits BIGINT
) WITH (
    connector = 'kafka',
    format = 'json',
    type = 'sink',
    bootstrap_servers = 'localhost:9092',
    topic = 'features'
);

INSERT INTO features
SELECT window.end, path, count
FROM (
    SELECT count(*) AS count, path,
           hop(interval '5 seconds', '1 minute') AS window
    FROM events
    GROUP BY path, window
);

hop(interval '5 seconds', '1 minute') is Arroyo’s sliding-window sugar — a one-minute window advanced every five seconds. Produce a few JSON events to the events topic and the features topic starts receiving per-minute counts continuously, checkpointed against failure.

Honest Limits

No source tour can prove what the code does not show, so the claims below are restricted to what the README states and what the checked-out tree reveals:

  • Performance: the README claims scaling “up to millions of events per second”; that is a project claim, and we ran no benchmarks for this tour.
  • Control plane: the API and controller expect Postgres or SQLite (DatabaseType dispatch in main.rs at L311); the single-binary cluster command embeds API, compiler, and controller together (start_control_plane, L445).
  • WASM: the graph model still defines WasmUDF types (datastream lib.rs, L49), but the UDF host we traced on master loads dynamic libraries and Python; we did not find a WASM executor wired into the runtime crates we read, so treat WASM UDFs as legacy surface, not a current feature path.
  • Exactly-once semantics: the two-phase commit machinery is real, but end-to-end guarantees depend on each sink’s connector implementation; the filesystem sink, for instance, carries its own two-phase committer.
  • Scheduling: the controller includes a Kubernetes scheduler (crates/arroyo-controller/src/schedulers/kubernetes/), but we only read code — no cluster deployments were exercised here.
  • This article is a source tour of one snapshot of master; APIs move fast, so anchor to the line links rather than quoting behavior from memory.
entry.summary: A guided tour through the Arroyo source tree: how Rust, DataFusion and Arrow turn SQL over Kafka topics into a checkpointed distributed dataflow.

entry.title: Bytewax Under the Hood: A Source Tour of Python Stream Processing on a Rust Timely Core

link.title: Bytewax Under the Hood: A Source Tour of Python Stream Processing on a Rust Timely Core

entry.content:
Every serious ML system eventually hits the same wall: the features that feed your model have to be computed continuously, on live data, with state that survives crashes. Batch scoring is not enough once tokens, clicks, sensor readings, or order events arrive per second. Bytewax attacks exactly this gap — it is a Python-native stream processing framework whose execution engine is written in Rust on top of Timely Dataflow. You express a dataflow with ordinary Python functions and operators, and a compiled extension distributes that computation across workers and processes.

What makes Bytewax interesting as a codebase, compared with the engines we have toured before such as Arroyo and RisingWave, is that the Python API is not a thin shell over an embedded SQL planner. Instead, the Dataflow object you build in Python is a declarative record of steps, and Rust code walks that record and reconstructs the whole thing as Timely operators. The language boundary is a compiler boundary: Python describes, Rust executes. That split — plus an SQLite-backed recovery journal and a confluent-kafka connector — is what we traced in the source.

We cloned bytewax/bytewax at branch main and read three areas: pysrc/bytewax (the Python package), src (the Rust crate), and examples. The two diagrams below were generated from the actual file tree, and every symbol cited in this post was verified against the checkout — line numbers anchor claims so you can jump straight from this page into the source.

Overview: the Python operator API and connectors on the left, the CLI entry points in the middle, and the Rust Timely core plus recovery journal on the right.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • wordcount.py, L17 is the smallest complete dataflow: op.input, op.map, op.flat_map, op.count_final, op.output — five calls, one running program.
  • Dataflow, L178 is a dataclass that records the operator tree, and Stream, L214 is the typed handle that links one step’s output to the next step’s input.
  • map, L2499 sits in the operator library; each public operator is a decorated function that appends a step to the flow and returns a new Stream.
  • window, L1256 adds event-time windows on top, driven by an EventClock, L361 with watermarks and a TumblingWindower, L897 (sliding and session windowers share the same interface).
  • FixedPartitionedSource, L144 is the source contract for partitioned inputs; KafkaSource, L340 implements it over confluent-kafka.
  • run.py, L343 is what executes when you type python -m bytewax.run: argparse parses workers, addresses, and recovery flags, imports your flow, then hands everything to Rust cli_main.
  • run_main, L114 and cluster_main, L239 are the Rust entry points, registered into the _bytewax PyO3 module at mod_bytewax, L26.
  • build_production_dataflow, L255 is the heart of execution: it walks the Python step tree and constructs real Timely operators.
  • write_recovery, L1707 persists state snapshots into the journal, and load_snaps, L1638 replays them on restart.

Detail: from the Python `Dataflow` model through the operator API and Kafka connector, across the PyO3 bridge into the Timely worker, dispatch, and the SQLite recovery journal.

The Operator API: Where Python Meets the Core

The public surface lives in pysrc/bytewax. Stateless operators such as map, filter, and flat_map wrap a Python callable and are almost self-explanatory. The stateful half is more instructive. stateful, L1067 takes a builder and asks you to implement the StatefulLogic, L919 abstract class: on_item processes one item per key, on_notify fires timers, and snapshot returns picklable state. That last method is not decoration — it is the exact hook the recovery journal uses. Internally, every stateful operator, including join at join, L2326 and the windowing operator, compiles down to a single core primitive: stateful_batch, L797, wrapped by the StatefulBatchLogic, L594 adapter. One primitive, snapshotted one way, powers the whole stateful surface.

The @operator decorator itself does more than registration: it type-checks ports, generates stable step IDs, and lets operators compose. Composite operators are real: op.collect at collect, L1150 and fold_final at fold_final, L1946 are written against StatefulLogic, the same primitives you would use, so reading the library source doubles as a tutorial for writing your own operators. Keyed streams are the state boundary — key_on, L2377 converts any stream into a KeyedStream, and every stateful operator requires one, which is why per-key routing is visible in the execution core rather than hidden as an implementation detail. For read-mostly enrichment, enrich_cached, L1316 pairs a TTL cache with a lookup function so reference data does not have to flow through the stream.

Inside the Timely Execution Core

The src directory is a Rust crate compiled as a PyO3 extension module named _bytewax. When run_main receives your flow, it extracts the Python Dataflow into a Rust wrapper (dataflow.rs, L8) and starts a Timely computation. Worker, L40 then drives the event loop until the probe reports done — epochs advance on a configurable interval, which is how time is coordinated across workers.

The translation step is build_production_dataflow, L255. It pushes steps onto a stack and dispatches on core operator names: input, inspect_debug, merge, output, redistribute, and stateful_batch (the arm is at worker.rs, L447). For input, it checks whether the Python source object is a fixed-partitioned or dynamic source and calls the matching builder; for stateful_batch, it hands control to the Rust-side Timely operator at operators.rs, L445, which batches items per epoch, calls into your Python logic, and drains snapshot bytes for recovery. One subtlety visible in the builder is that composite Python operators never reach this dispatch directly: when the step on the stack is not a core operator, the builder pops its substeps at worker.rs, L468 and pushes them back for expansion, so by the time the stack unwinds, every node in the Timely graph is one of a handful of primitives. Multi-process runs go through cluster_main, L239, with worker counts parsed into WorkerCount, L309. If you want the visual version of your own flow, to_mermaid, L302 renders the step graph as Mermaid.

Recovery: an SQLite Journal of Epochs

Bytewax’s fault tolerance is epoch-based. Every stateful operator emits a snapshot each epoch; those snapshot streams are concatenated and fed to write_recovery, L1707, which writes them through per-partition writers into SQLite databases configured by RecoveryConfig, L319. The schema is managed with SQLite migrations, and each part also records execution metadata and frontier information so a restarted cluster can agree on where to resume. On restart, load_snaps, L1638 streams the snapshots back before the resume epoch, and build_production_dataflow wires them into each operator’s initial state — so a crash costs you at most the last epoch interval, not the whole run. Writing is batched through a RecoveryCommitter, L943 that flushes committed epoch data, and a test named gc_leaves_only_final_snap at recovery.rs, L992 documents the retention rule the journal applies when pruning. The Python side stays thin: passing -r <dir> plus -s and -b intervals makes run.py, L343 construct the config that crosses the bridge.

Kafka In, Insights Out

The connector package wraps confluent-kafka, the Python client over librdkafka. KafkaSource, L340 manages one consumer per partition, resumes from committed offsets, and emits KafkaSourceMessage, L92 records that carry key, value, offset, and timestamp. The ergonomic layer is the operator pair at kafka.input, L91 and output, which build the source and KafkaSink, L537 in one call. Deserialization is its own layer: the operators deserialize_key, deserialize_value, and deserialize, L273 turn raw bytes into JSON or Python objects on the stream, with serialize and friends at serialize, L396 on the way out, so byte handling never leaks into your business logic. Since the connector is just an implementation of the source ABCs, swapping brokers is a config change — our Kafka and Redpanda source tours cover the server side of that pairing.

From Install to Your First Model

Start with pip install bytewax. Save the wordcount example as wordcount.py, then run it with python -m bytewax.run wordcount.py; add -w 2 to run two workers in one process, or pass --addresses and --process-id to form a cluster across machines. For serving an ML model on a stream, the pattern from the source is direct: op.input from KafkaSource, op.map to deserialize and call your model (an ONNX or scikit-learn scorer inside a plain Python function), op.key_on followed by op.stateful to maintain per-user features, then op.output back to Kafka. waxctl df deploy packages the same flow file for Kubernetes deployments, and the repository’s own examples directory covers joins, windowing, and Redpanda serdes beyond wordcount. To inspect what you built, python -m bytewax.visualize prints the flow as Mermaid text you can paste into a README.

Honest Limits

Everything above was verified by reading the repository at main on 2026-11-04; we ran no benchmarks and claim none. A few practical caveats surface in the source itself. First, recovery is opt-in and requires all three flags — -r, -s, and -b — otherwise the CLI refuses to start, so out of the box your dataflow state is ephemeral. Second, KafkaSink extends DynamicSink, the stateless sink contract, and the recovery machinery in src/recovery.rs tracks stateful operators — the journal protects your aggregation state, while output delivery semantics depend on the sink implementation. Third, the Rust internals are pub(crate): the Python API is the only supported contract, so operator behavior can shift between releases; the changelog and migration guide are worth reading before upgrading. Finally, Bytewax is a dataflow engine, not a SQL database — if you want streaming SQL instead of Python operators, our earlier tours of Arroyo and RisingWave cover that style of engine.
entry.summary: A source tour of bytewax/bytewax showing how the Python operator API compiles down to Timely Dataflow operators in Rust, with an SQLite recovery journal and confluent-kafka connectors.

entry.title: Inside Apache Druid: A Java Source Tour of Streaming Ingestion, Segments, and the Broker Query Layer

link.title: Inside Apache Druid: A Java Source Tour of Streaming Ingestion, Segments, and the Broker Query Layer

entry.content:
When you train a model, the easy part is the model. The hard part is everything that happens after it starts serving: millions of prediction events, feature distributions drifting by the hour, error rates that spike in ways your offline dashboards never see. Answering “how has the model behaved over the last five minutes?” at that event volume is exactly the job Apache Druid was built for — a high performance, real-time analytics database whose own README describes its mission as reducing “time to insight and action.” Every inference endpoint that logs its calls can become a Druid datasource, and Druid’s columnar, time-partitioned storage makes the resulting dashboards fast even under high concurrency.

Druid also occupies a sweet spot in the streaming ecosystem. Records typically arrive from a distributed log — whether that is Kafka-compatible Redpanda, as covered in our /redpanda/ tour, or Pulsar, whose tiered architecture we explored in /pulsar/ — while SQL-style stream engines like the one in /risingwave/ materialize views on top of those logs. Druid differs from both: it is not a processing engine but a database, one that ingests events continuously, packs them into immutable columnar segments, and serves interactive queries seconds after the bytes land. And compared with single-node time-series stores like /questdb/, Druid scales horizontally by design: any node can ingest, any node can query, and a coordinator keeps the data spread evenly.

This post is a source tour, not a tutorial-by-rumor. Everything cited below was verified against a depth-1 checkout of apache/druid on branch master, mostly in three modules: indexing-service (the ingestion runtime), server (broker, coordinator, and data-node plumbing), and processing (segments and the native query engine). The two diagrams were generated from the actual file tree, and every symbol and line number in this article exists in the code as of commit 79fb6155 on the default branch.

Figure 1 — Overview: the overlord runs ingestion tasks, tasks write segments, the broker fans queries out to the data nodes that serve those segments, and the coordinator rebalances the whole thing. Generated from the repository tree.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts at the OverlordResource, L114, the REST face of the overlord where ingestion tasks are submitted, inspected, and shut down.
  • TaskMaster, L42 elects the overlord leader and owns the queue that actually gets work done; only one node leads at a time.
  • The queue itself, TaskQueue, L108, holds waiting and running tasks, acquires locks, and drives them to completion in a management loop.
  • Streaming work enters through SeekableStreamIndexTaskRunner, L151, the read-index-push loop shared by Kafka and Kinesis ingestion.
  • Rows buffer in IncrementalIndex, L112, an in-memory sink that applies rollup before anything is persisted.
  • On the read side, QueryResource, L75 accepts native query JSON over HTTP, and QueryLifecycle, L89 walks a query through initialize, authorize, and execute.
  • ClientQuerySegmentWalker, L98 is the broker’s walker: it splits a query across the cluster and merges partial results.
  • Data nodes answer through ServerManager, L100, which maps segment descriptors to the loaded segments it serves.
  • Above it all, DruidCoordinator, L118 runs the periodic duties loop that keeps segments replicated and balanced.

Figure 2 — Detail: task submission, the runner hierarchy, the streaming task loop, the segment life cycle from IncrementalIndex to QueryableIndex, the query engine chain, and the coordinator's balancing stack.

Inside the Ingestion Task Runtime

Druid treats ingestion as a set of concurrent, retryable units of work. The contract is the Task, L90 interface, which declares the datasources a task touches, the locks it needs, and its run method. Submission lands in TaskQueue, whose add method at L526 registers the task, and whose management loop starts at L220, periodically pushing waiting tasks into runners. Before a task can write, the queue asks TaskLockbox, L89 for segment locks, which is how two tasks ingesting overlapping intervals are prevented from clobbering each other.

Where does the task actually execute? That is pluggable via TaskRunner, L44. Locally, ThreadingTaskRunner, L92 runs tasks in-process on threads, while ForkingTaskRunner, L98 forks a fresh JVM per task so a misbehaving parser cannot take down the middle manager. In a distributed setup the middle manager exposes its slots through WorkerTaskManager, L86, and the overlord assigns remotely — the HTTP-based runner’s startup lives at HttpRemoteTaskRunner, L229. Long-running streaming ingest is not a bare task but a supervisor: SupervisorManager, L305 starts and monitors them, and the generic supervisor’s start method at SeekableStreamSupervisor, L1318 spawns a partition task per replica set, tracks offsets, and replaces failed tasks.

The Segment Storage Model

Druid’s read speed comes from how it stores data, not from any query-time magic. The atomic unit is a segment: rows for one time interval, rolled up, indexed by column, and written once. The metadata record is DataSegment, L62, an immutable object describing the interval, version, shard spec, dimensions, metrics, and deep-storage location. While a task is ingesting, rows live in IncrementalIndex — its class declaration at L112 shows it implementing the row selector and column inspector interfaces that the engine needs even before persistence.

Once a segment is pushed, it is opened as a QueryableIndex, L47, the read-only columnar view, wrapped by QueryableIndexSegment, L36, which implements the base Segment, L40 interface. Handing segments to queries is a timeline problem: VersionedIntervalTimeline, L75 stores segment shards per interval and version so that newer data shadows older data atomically — its add method at L208 is where a published segment becomes visible. On a data node, SegmentManager, L69 opens segments from deep storage (see loadSegment), while SegmentLoadDropHandler, L61 is the receiver for the coordinator’s load and drop commands, with addSegment handling the local copy.

The Broker and the Query Layer

A native Druid query is JSON in, JSON out. The HTTP surface is QueryResource; its doPost handler at L161 hands the parsed query to QueryLifecycle, L89, a state machine whose initialize fixes the query ID and context, authorize enforces datasource ACLs, and execute at L416 produces the response sequence. The broker does not compute results itself: ClientQuerySegmentWalker at L98 walks the query tree, issuing subqueries against the cluster and merging partials — including the subquery handling that lets one query feed another.

On each data node, ServerManager, L100 resolves requested segment descriptors into per-segment query runners: see getQueryRunnerForSegments at L184. Each query type gets its own execution strategy from QueryRunnerFactory, L31, paired with a QueryToolChest, L46 that defines merging and result semantics. Three classic engines show the pattern: TimeseriesQuery, L60 for time-bucketed aggregates, GroupByQuery, L90 for multi-dimensional grouping, and TopNQuery, L52 for ranked lists — the same aggregation vocabulary you would use to slice a model’s prediction log by feature bucket.

The Coordinator: Balance Without Drama

Ingestion writes segments; someone has to decide where they live and how many copies exist. That is DruidCoordinator, L118, whose start method at L368 spins up the periodic duty services. One key duty is BalanceSegments, L39, whose run at L51 feeds the cluster’s servers and segments into a BalancerStrategy, L35 and issues the resulting moves. The default cost model is interesting to read: CostBalancerStrategy, L53 prices two segments together based on how much their time intervals overlap, with a decay half-life of 24 hours visible at L57 — recent segments are deliberately spread wider than old, cold ones. computeJointSegmentsCost at L102 does the math, and findDestinationServerToMoveSegment at L239 picks the least-cost destination when a move is needed. For an ML platform, that behavior matters: your busiest dashboard window — say, the last hour of prediction events — gets spread across the most servers precisely when you are staring at it.

From Install to Your First Model

The fastest path is the documented quickstart: grab a release from the Apache Druid downloads page or run the official Docker image (apache/druid on Docker Hub), then follow the local or Docker quickstart linked from the README. If you prefer starting from this exact source tree, the single-server scripts are in the repo: examples/bin/start-micro-quickstart (small trial config under examples/conf/druid/single-server/micro-quickstart/) or examples/bin/start-nano-quickstart. Once the services are up, open the built-in web console: use the point-and-click loader to ingest a sample stream or file as a datasource — your model’s prediction log in JSON is a perfectly good first one — then watch tasks and supervisors under the tasks view. Finish in the query workbench by issuing DruidSQL: a SELECT with TIME_FLOOR on the timestamp and an aggregator per feature bucket gives you a live slice of serving behavior, backed by the same engine classes described above. Connecting your Kafka-compatible log takes one supervisor spec, and both of the streaming transports we compared earlier are first-class citizens here.

Honest Limits

Everything above comes from the code and README; nothing here is a benchmark, and none of the performance adjectives should be read as measurements. Some boundaries of this tour: it covers the native query classes, not the SQL planner, which lives in modules I did not read; building Druid from source requires JDK 25 per the README, so reproducing the line numbers means checking out master at the same commit rather than an arbitrary older tag; the 24-hour cost half-life in the balancer is a code constant whose operational effect I have not tested; and micro-quickstart is explicitly a single-server trial configuration, not a sizing recommendation for production fleets. If your workload fits on one box, a lean single-node time-series store will be simpler to run; Druid’s payoff starts when data and query volume outgrow any single machine.
entry.summary: A source-level walkthrough of Apache Druid's ingestion task runtime, immutable segment storage model, broker query fan-out, and coordinator balancing, verified against the Java code on master.

entry.title: Inside Materialize: A Source Tour of the Rust Streaming Database That Compiles SQL into Dataflows

link.title: Inside Materialize: A Source Tour of the Rust Streaming Database That Compiles SQL into Dataflows

entry.content:
If you have ever wired an ML feature store, you know the pain: features are computed offline, batched into a table, and served stale by the time your model reads them. Materialize attacks that problem from an unusual direction — it is a PostgreSQL-compatible database that keeps your SQL views continuously, transactionally up to date as the underlying data changes. Its own README pitches exactly the use case this blog cares about: delivering fresh context for AI and RAG applications, operational dashboards, and real-time products, without hand-rolling custom streaming plumbing. The payoff is one system acting as a cache, a streaming job, and a warehouse at the same time.

What makes Materialize special is not “another streaming engine”. RisingWave, which we toured earlier this week, walks a similar road; Redpanda gives you the event log underneath; but Materialize’s pitch is correctness: every query answer is the correct result on some specific, recent version of your data, even for joins across multiple upstream systems, and never an approximate or eventually consistent one. Under the hood it recasts your SQL as dataflows — incremental, reactive computation graphs built on the timely and differential dataflow libraries, the same research lineage that powers Materialize’s niche in the streaming space.

This post is a source tour of MaterializeInc/materialize (Rust, branch main). We will walk four crates that together form the whole machine: adapter (the coordinator that speaks SQL), storage (ingestion from Kafka and Postgres CDC), compute (timely/differential workers that maintain views), and persist (durable storage). Two diagrams anchor the tour — an overview first, then a detail view with the actual files and entry points.

Overview: the coordinator (adapter crate) drives storage and compute clusters; both layers land their data in the persist layer, which reduces to Blob and Consensus abstractions.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The Coordinator, L1908 is the heart of the SQL layer. It bootstraps the environment, owns the catalog, and multiplexes every client command through one message loop — the same process that serves the PostgreSQL wire protocol.
  • DDL does not execute imperatively. Statements are sequenced: sequence_create_source, L634 shows the staged pattern, where each plan step is deterministic and resumable.
  • Provisioning is centralized in the cluster controller. ClusterControllerRequest, L66 models the request vocabulary for starting, resizing, and routing to storage and compute replicas.
  • On the ingestion side, serve, L56 is the entry point of the storaged process, which renders every source and sink assigned to a storage cluster.
  • Source-native progress is normalized by ReclockOperator, L36, which maps Kafka offsets and Postgres LSNs onto Materialize’s timestamp timeline.
  • For queries, serve, L184 boots the timely worker set of a compute replica, and ComputeState, L177 is the per-worker registry of dataflows, arrangements, peeks, and subscriptions.
  • Everything durable bottoms out in two abstractions: Blob, L566 for immutable, versioned buffers, and Consensus, L442 for a linearizable compare-and-swap log.

Detail: per-crate call graph with verified file paths — from statement sequencing and timestamp selection down to Avro decoding, RocksDB upsert state, parquet-encoded trace batches, and hedged blob reads.

The Coordinator: Where SQL Meets Streaming

The adapter crate is the brain. When a client connects, it looks exactly like a Postgres server on the wire, but CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW does something no ordinary database does: it registers a long-lived dataflow instead of snapshotting a result. The coordinator’s bootstrap, L2395 replays the catalog on startup, then hands each incoming statement to the sequencer. For materialized views specifically, create_materialized_view_finish, L563 optimizes the query, installs the dataflow in a compute cluster, and commits the definition to the catalog — in that order, atomically.

Query time is the subtle part. A SELECT must answer at a single logical timestamp where all its inputs are readable. TimestampDetermination, L761 is the structure that pins a query to such an as-of time, and PeekClient, L64 then races the peek out to replicas. If one replica is slow or fails, another answers — multi-active replication falls out of the design rather than being bolted on.

Ingestion: Kafka and Postgres CDC in storaged

The storage crate turns external systems into timestamped collections. The shape of each source is the same three-stage composition: read raw updates, decode them into typed rows, then reclock source-native progress into Materialize timestamps. Kafka topics arrive as partition readers — KafkaSourceReader, L110 — with an Avro path in AvroDecoderState, L16 that understands Confluent schema-registry payloads. For upsert semantics, keyed state is spilled to RocksDB, L22, so a backfill of a huge topic does not have to fit in RAM.

The CDC sources are the ones your AI feature work will likely use. ensure_replication_slot, L442 takes a consistent snapshot of your tables and then tails Postgres’ logical replication stream, using the LSN as native progress. MySQL replication follows the same pattern in src/storage/src/source/mysql/. All of this per-worker wiring is coordinated by StorageState, L300, which also drives the async storage worker that publishes progress. If you run Redpanda or Kafka in your stack, this is the code that consumes them; we benchmarked those brokers separately on this blog.

Compute: Timely Workers, Arrangements, Differential Joins

The compute crate is where differential dataflow earns its keep. The core idea is compact enough for a paragraph: every collection is a set of (data, time, diff) triples, and every operator — join, reduce, top-k — is written once against that abstraction so it can recompute only what changed, when logical time advances along a partial order. That is why Materialize can maintain a multi-way join over live CDC streams without recomputing the world on every update, and why queries have coherent answers instead of tearing across partial updates. build_compute_dataflow, L210 lowers an optimized plan into operators, with render_plan, L1161 dispatching each operator kind — joins, reduces, top-k — to its implementation. The resulting arrangements (indexed, incrementally maintainable multisets) are kept alive and compacted by TraceManager, L33.

Reads and outputs flow through the same state machine. One-shot SELECTs run via serve_index_peek, L1193, which waits until the arrangement’s frontier passes the query’s as-of time. Continuous outputs use sinks: persist_sink, L240 streams a materialized view’s output into durable shards, and subscribe, L83 implements the SUBSCRIBE tail protocol. Memory pressure is not an afterthought — start_limiter, L41 reserves global budgets so a replica degrades predictably instead of getting OOM-killed mid-query.

Persist: Blob and Consensus

Durability is deliberately two-trait simple. Blob, L566 stores immutable buffers; Consensus, L442 provides a linearizable CAS over a short log that records each shard’s current state and upper frontier. Implementations swap by URL scheme: FileBlob, L45 for single-node local runs (CRC-checked), Postgres/CRDB-backed consensus and S3/GCS/Azure blobs for cloud deployments — MinIO works fine as the S3 endpoint for experiments.

Two production details are worth stealing for your own systems. First, tail latency: HedgedBlob, L236 fires a second read when the first is slow, hiding object-storage hiccups. Second, columnar efficiency: encode_trace_parquet, L43 packs trace batches into parquet before they land in blobs, which is what makes “near-infinite storage” in the README more than marketing.

From Install to Your First Model

Here is the fastest loop, all of it straight from the repository’s README. Grab the community edition from materialize.com/download (free forever under 24 GiB of memory and 48 GiB of disk), run materialized or the Docker image, and point psql at it — it speaks the PostgreSQL protocol, so any driver works. Then create a demo source and a materialized view:

CREATE SOURCE tpch
  FROM LOAD GENERATOR TPCH (SCALE FACTOR 1)
  FOR ALL TABLES;

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW tpch_q15 AS
  SELECT s_suppkey, s_name, s_address, s_phone, total_revenue
  FROM supplier, revenue
  WHERE s_suppkey = supplier_no
    AND total_revenue = (SELECT max(total_revenue) FROM revenue);

CREATE INDEX tpch_q15_idx ON tpch_q15 (s_suppkey);

The load generator streams inserts, updates, and deletes on the underlying tables, and Materialize keeps tpch_q15 incrementally updated the whole time. SELECT * FROM tpch_q15 returns current results immediately — no REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW, no cache invalidation, no cron. Getting data out is symmetric: the README documents both pull-based access through any PostgreSQL-compatible driver and push-based tails — SUBSCRIBE streams every change to a view as it lands, and sinks can forward the same updates to a Kafka topic or copy them to object storage.

For an ML serving stack, the pattern maps directly: define your features as views over CDC sources, let the coordinator and compute workers maintain them continuously, and have your Python inference service query them like an ordinary Postgres database — or tail them with SUBSCRIBE for streaming inference.

Honest Limits

Everything above comes from the README and the source; none of it is a benchmark, and we ran none. Limits worth knowing before you build: the community edition’s free tier is bounded by those 24/48 GiB figures — real production scale historically means the managed cloud or an enterprise deployment. The SQL dialect is a large but not complete subset of PostgreSQL; check the docs for the functions you rely on. Persist’s Consensus currently targets Postgres/CockroachDB and blobs target the big three object stores, so fully air-gapped, single-binary deployments trade you back into local file durability. And while the load generators are excellent for demos, your own Postgres CDC source will need a replication slot — plan the primary’s disk and wal_keep settings accordingly, or the source will misbehave at snapshot time. Finally, this tour reflects branch main at a point in time; the codebase moves fast, and file paths will drift. Materialize maintains views; it does not replace a broker — you still want Kafka or Redpanda upstream and a serving layer downstream, and Materialize is the correctness-preserving middle that makes both smarter.
entry.summary: A guided tour of the Materialize Rust source, from the SQL coordinator and timely dataflow workers to Postgres CDC sources and durable persist shards.

entry.title: Inside Apache Pinot: A Java Source Tour of Segments, Broker Routing and the Realtime Consuming Path

link.title: Inside Apache Pinot: A Java Source Tour of Segments, Broker Routing and the Realtime Consuming Path

entry.content:
Recommendation and personalization models live or die by how fresh their inputs are. A ranking model that cannot see the last five minutes of user behavior is quietly optimizing the past, and an LLM ops dashboard that answers in seconds instead of milliseconds gets ignored by on-call engineers. Apache Pinot is the real-time OLAP datastore built for exactly this gap: it ingests streams as they arrive, indexes everything column-wise, and answers aggregations over billions of rows in the low hundreds of milliseconds. Originally open-sourced by LinkedIn and now a top-level Apache project, it sits in the serving layer that makes “fresh features” and “fresh monitoring” affordable at scale — the same freshness guarantee that streaming databases like /risingwave/ push into materialized views, except Pinot pushes it down into storage and serving.

What makes Pinot fascinating to read at the source level is how small its core ideas are. Everything a query touches is a segment: an immutable, column-oriented, dictionary-encoded chunk of rows. The broker does almost no per-query computation beyond compiling SQL, pruning segments, and choosing which servers get the fan-out. And the realtime path — the low-level consumer, LLC for short — continuously converts a stream partition into the exact same segment format on the fly, so serving code never needs to know whether a row arrived three minutes ago or three weeks ago. That symmetry is the property worth internalizing: one index format, one query execution path, two ingestion modes.

This post walks through that architecture in Java source, reading the master branch of apache/pinot across four modules: pinot-broker (request handling and routing), pinot-server (the query worker), pinot-core (scheduling, execution, and the realtime managers), and pinot-segment-local (segment creation and on-disk store). Line references point at the tree head at the time of writing, so they will drift as the code moves — the structure, though, has been stable for years.

The overview graph: a query flows from broker compile-and-route into the server query path, while the realtime consumption loop feeds rows into mutable segments that get sealed, committed, uploaded and routed back into the query path.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • A SQL request lands in BaseSingleStageBrokerRequestHandler, L434, where doHandleRequest compiles the query, validates access, and prepares the fan-out.
  • The broker asks BaseBrokerRoutingManager, L1216 for a RoutingTable; buildRouting at L728 rebuilds those entries whenever Helix reports segment or instance changes.
  • Before any server is involved, TimeSegmentPruner, L160 drops segments whose time range falls outside the query, using the watermark published by TimeBoundaryManager, L285.
  • Server choice per segment is a routing concern too: BalancedInstanceSelector, L44 spreads segments across healthy servers, selected via InstanceSelectorFactory, L43.
  • On each server, the request arrives at WorkerQueryServer, L36, gets admitted by QueryScheduler, L175, and is executed by ServerQueryExecutorV1Impl, L157.
  • The realtime loop starts at RealtimeTableDataManager, L744, which constructs one RealtimeSegmentDataManager, L129 per stream partition.
  • Inside it, PartitionConsumer.run at L794 pulls messages and pushes every row into MutableSegmentImpl, L638, where dictionary, forward, and inverted indexes update in memory.
  • When the segment fills up, SegmentCommitterFactory, L53 builds a committer and Server2ControllerSegmentUploader, L40 ships the sealed segment off — after which it becomes routable, closing the loop.

The detail graph adds the broker routing internals, server boot wiring, the LLC consumption loop with its commit and upload variants, and the segment build stack.

Segments: the unit of storage and query

Pinot’s storage model has one load-bearing abstraction: a segment is a self-contained, immutable mini-table. Offline tables get segments built from batch jobs; realtime tables get them built from live consumption; queries treat both identically. The batch build path lives in SegmentIndexCreationDriverImpl, L249, whose build method pulls rows through a record reader and hands each column to SegmentColumnarIndexCreator, L55. Per row, indexRow feeds the value into a dictionary creator — see SegmentDictionaryCreator, L58 — plus the forward index writers, and builds inverted indexes for indexed columns. This is why filters and group-bys are cheap: a WHERE color = 'red' becomes a dictionary lookup plus a bitmap intersection, not a scan.

The on-disk layout has two flavors, and the difference matters for ops. The file-per-index layout is managed by SegmentLocalFSDirectory, L51, while SingleFileIndexDirectory, L76 packs all indexes of a segment into one file — fewer inodes and a friendlier upload unit for deep stores. The consuming path reuses the very same index creators: MutableSegmentImpl, L142 hosts the mutable versions so that a segment being written right now is already indexed and already queryable. Architecturally, this is the closest cousin to Druid, which chunks time into immutable segments too — our /druid/ tour covers that overlap in detail.

The realtime consuming path (LLC)

The realtime side is where Pinot earns the “real-time” in its name, and the class that carries it is RealtimeSegmentDataManager, L129. Each instance owns one stream partition group and runs PartitionConsumer (declared at L793); its run loop calls consumeLoop at L483 repeatedly until end-of-segment criteria are met — a row-count or time threshold, or an idle timeout on quiet topics. Consumption is low-level by design: the server reads from an explicit partition and offset range rather than a consumer group, which removes group-rebalancing storms from the critical path. The stream adapter is pluggable, so Kafka and Pulsar — see our /pulsar/ deep dive — plug in behind the same interfaces.

Coordination between consumers on the same server is enforced by ConsumerCoordinator, L93, whose acquire grants a per-partition semaphore and whose release at L119 hands it to the next segment — exactly one consumer per partition, per server. When the consuming segment is full, the flow is the interesting part: buildSegmentForCommit at L1113 triggers buildSegmentInternal at L1208, which converts the in-memory mutable segment into an immutable one using the same creators from the previous section. Because that build can outlast the controller’s lease, SegmentBuildTimeLeaseExtender, L40 keeps renewing it. Then createSegmentCommitter, built at SegmentCommitterFactory, L53, uploads the artifact — either straight to the controller via Server2ControllerSegmentUploader, L40 or directly to a deep store with PinotFSSegmentUploader, L44. Once the controller marks the segment ONLINE, the broker’s buildRouting picks it up and queries start hitting the sealed copy while the next consuming segment is already filling.

Broker routing and query planning

The broker’s job is best understood as “make every query touch as few servers and segments as possible.” Compilation happens in compileRequest at BaseSingleStageBrokerRequestHandler, L1100, where Calcite-parsed SQL becomes a PinotQuery and optimizer passes rewrite filters and aggregations. Routing then narrows the segment set twice: once at the broker with the pruners described above, and once on each server, where SegmentPrunerService, L85 applies value-based and bloom-filter pruners against actual segment metadata. Execution per segment comes from a Plan produced by the PlanMaker, L35 interface — an operator tree of scans, transforms, and aggregations run inside ServerQueryExecutorV1Impl, L157. The single-stage responses stream back over pooled connections handled by SingleConnectionBrokerRequestHandler, L92, which merges partial DataTable results into the final response. Admission control lives server-side in processQueryAndSerializeResponse at QueryScheduler, L175, backed by a multi-level priority queue so a burst of cheap dashboards cannot starve expensive model-monitoring queries. The selector choice itself is per-table configuration: the factory dispatches on the table’s routing config between balanced routing at L131, replica-group routing at L103 — which co-locates a query’s segments on a replica group to keep fan-out width down — plus strict replica-group and multi-stage variants. The trade-off is easy to state: balanced routing maximizes the number of servers that can absorb a query; replica-group routing minimizes cross-server traffic and tail latency for wide scans.

From Install to Your First Model

Getting a cluster running for experiments is a single-JVM affair. The README’s developer path is: clone the repo, build with ./mvnw clean install -DskipTests -Pbin-dist -Pbuild-shaded-jar (the project now requires JDK 25+ to build and run, while Java/JDBC clients stay on Java 11 bytecode), then from the build/ directory run bin/quick-start-batch.sh. That boots the batch Quick Demo — controller, broker, and server in one process with a sample dataset already loaded, and the official Quick Demo docs walk you through the query console and your first SQL statements. For streaming, the docs’ stream quick-start does the same against a bundled topic, which is the closest analogue to pointing Pinot at your own event stream. For an AI workload, the natural first experiment is a realtime table over your model’s inference logs: define a schema with the feature columns and a time column, point the table at your topic, and query percentiles of latency per model version with a GROUP BY — the same primitives the consumption loop above has been indexing since the first message arrived.

Honest Limits

Everything above comes from reading the master tree (head 660962f at the time of writing) and the project README; no benchmarks were run for this post, so treat any performance expectations as untested here. The tour is also deliberately partial: it covers four modules, leaving the controller (segment assignment and the Helix state machines), minions, and the plugin ecosystem unread — the streaming adapters, for instance, live in separate plugin modules that merely implement interfaces referenced by the code shown here. Two operational limits are nonetheless visible directly in the source. First, realtime ingestion pays its index cost immediately: every row updates the mutable dictionaries and indexes in MutableSegmentImpl’s index method, L638, so wide schemas with high-cardinality strings are expensive the moment they arrive, not just at query time. Second, the segment build is a serialized step per partition — the code explicitly acquires a semaphore before building — which means pathological build times require the lease extension at SegmentBuildTimeLeaseExtender, L40 to avoid commit failures. And a scope caveat: Pinot is a general OLAP engine, not a time-series-first store; for pure high-frequency metrics ingestion with a different storage trade-off, compare with /questdb/ before choosing.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of Apache Pinot showing how immutable segments, broker routing and the low-level consumer turn streams into millisecond analytics for AI systems.
